bib.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models. Zhengxuan Wu*, Aryaman Arora*, Zheng Wang, Atticus Geiger, Dan Jurafsky, Christopher D. Manning, Christopher Potts (Stanford, Pr(Ai)2R). arXiv 2404.03592v3, 22 May 2024. Marked "Preprint. Under review." (the NeurIPS 2024 version is not what this PDF says).

COVERAGE: 49 pages, 133,393 chars. Read in full: abstract, sections 1-6 (chars 0-37,500), appendix A (pyreft code), the D.2 tuning advice, D.3, E, F, G, H and the start of I (chars 69,300-121,500). Skimmed by section headings only, not read line by line: references, B (RED, activation addition, RepE), C (dataset details), D.1 (per-task hyperparameter tables), the rest of I (generation examples) and J (licences). Memorisation figures 3-10 and runtime figure 11 are plots, so only their captions were read. This is NOT an RL paper: it is parameter-efficient finetuning by learned representation interventions. It has no reward, policy or RL content, so check that generative-ai/05-RL is the right home.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- ReFT trains interventions on frozen-model hidden states instead of weight updates. LoReFT edits the residual stream inside a rank-r subspace.
  number: Phi(h) = h + R^T(Wh + b - Rh), with R in R^{r x d} having orthonormal rows
  setup: only {R, W, b} are learned and the LM is frozen. It builds on distributed interchange intervention (DII, eq. 1) and DAS. In DII, the "source" is the target Rs, which LoReFT replaces with a learned linear projection Wh+b.
  quote: "ΦLoReFT(h)= h+ R⊺(Wh+ b− Rh) (2)"
  where: p.4, sec 3.2

- LoReFT uses 15x-65x fewer parameters than LoRA.
  number: 15x-65x
  setup: against LoRA, across the evaluated models and benchmarks. Example: 0.031% trainable parameters on LLaMA-7B versus LoRA's 0.826%.
  quote: "learn interventions that are 15×–65× more parameter-efficient than LoRA"
  where: abstract

- Commonsense reasoning: LoReFT beats LoRA and DoRA with about 25x fewer parameters. Averages on the eight-task COMMONSENSE170K benchmark:

| Model | LoReFT | DiReFT | DoRA | LoRA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LLaMA-7B | 80.2 (0.031%) | 79.0 | 78.1 (0.838%) | 74.7 (0.826%) |
| LLaMA-13B | 83.3 | 82.2 | 81.5 | 80.5 |
| Llama-2 7B | 81.8 | 80.9 | 79.7 | 77.6 |
| Llama-3 8B | 86.6 (0.026%) | 85.4 | 85.2 | 80.8 |

  setup: single combined finetune on 170K examples. Scores are the mean of 3 seeds. Baseline numbers are copied from Liu et al. 2024c (DoRA paper), not rerun. Hyperparameters were tuned on a GSM8K dev split, with 6 epochs.
  quote: "LoReFT 0.031% 69.3 84.4 80.3 93.1 84.2 83.2 68.2 78.9 80.2"
  where: Table 1, p.7

- Instruction following: LoReFT reaches 85.60 win-rate on Alpaca-Eval v1.0, above full finetuning, LoRA and RED.
  number: 85.60 (LoReFT) and 84.85 (DiReFT) against 80.93 (FT), 81.48 (LoRA) and 81.69 (RED)
  setup: Llama-2 7B trained on Ultrafeedback. Judge is GPT-4 against text-davinci-003. LoReFT and DiReFT train 0.0039% of parameters, the same as RED. Mean of 2 seeds. Hyperparameters were tuned on Alpaca-52K with LLaMA-7B and a GPT-4 turbo judge.
  quote: "Llama-2 7B & LoReFT (ours) 0.0039% 85.60"
  where: Table 3, p.8
  also: with half the rank (0.0019%) it scores 84.12. With 1K examples it scores 81.91, and training on 1K examples takes 18 min on one A100 40G with ≈1MB of parameters on disk. The text says "achieves a win-rate within 1% of GPT-3.5 Turbo 1106" (86.30).

- GLUE: LoReFT is comparable to the best PEFTs at the smallest parameter counts.
  number: RoBERTa-base average 84.2 (0.015%) against LoRA 84.7 (0.239%), RED 84.3 and FT 85.6. RoBERTa-large average 88.2 (0.014%) against LoRA 88.1, RED 88.0 and FT 88.6.
  setup: mean of 5 seeds, on a held-out half of the validation set. Hyperparameters tuned per task. DiReFT is worse (83.2 base, 87.4 large).
  quote: "LoReFT (ours) 0.014% 89.2 96.2 90.1 68.0 94.1 88.5 87.5 91.6 88.2"
  where: Table 4, p.9

- Arithmetic reasoning is a loss. LoReFT is below LoRA and adapters.
  number: LLaMA-7B average 42.6 against LoRA 46.9, with GSM8K 26.0 against 37.5. LLaMA-13B average 49.6 against LoRA 51.1, with GSM8K 38.1 against 47.5.
  setup: MATH10K chain-of-thought training, four test sets, mean of 3 seeds. It beats prefix-tuning.
  quote: "We find that both LoReFT and DiReFT do not perform as well at arithmetic reasoning tasks compared to LoRA and adapters, but do outperform prefix-tuning."
  where: sec 4.3, Table 2, p.7-8
  also: the authors' guess is that "greater length necessarily reduces the effect of the intervention".

- The commonsense gain is not just extra epochs. LoReFT was trained longer than LoRA and DoRA, so the authors reran with matched epochs and effective batch size.
  number: LoReFT(e=3) averages 79.5 (7B) and 83.1 (13B)
  setup: 3 epochs with batch size 16, matching DoRA's number of gradient steps. On arithmetic, e=3 gives 39.3 (7B) and 48.8 (13B).
  quote: "With matched hyperparameters, LoReFT shows similar results by outperforming previous methods significantly on eight commonsense reasoning datasets."
  where: App D.3, Tables 14-15, p.29-30

- Ablation: dropping the orthogonality constraint or the difference term barely changes accuracy at equal parameter count. Input-independent versions are clearly worse.
  number: arithmetic average on LLaMA-7B is 42.6 (LoReFT), 42.9 (h+R^T(Wh+b)), 42.4 (non-orthogonal W1,W2 form) and 40.6 (DiReFT). Without Wh, it is 37.1 for h+R^T(b-Rh) and 31.3 for h+R^T b.
  setup: LLaMA-1 7B/13B, arithmetic benchmark, 3 seeds, LoReFT hyperparameters.
  quote: "variants with a similar number of trainable parameters also achieve similar performance to LoReFT across two models."
  where: App E, Table 17, p.32

- Hyperparameter advice from the authors (D.2).
  setup: advice, not a measured result
  quote: "Intervening on multiple positions delivers significant gains." / "Intervening on all layers first, and then shrink down." / "Higher rank may not entail better performance." / "Tie intervention weights as much as you can."
  where: App D.2, p.29. The paper suggests starting at rank 4 or lower than 32. Main method: intervene on p prefix and s suffix positions of the prompt only, so extra inference cost is a fixed number of positions, not tied to prompt length.

- Memorisation: a rank-1 intervention at one layer on the last prompt token can store long sequences.
  number: 100% recovery up to 2,048 tokens (LLaMA-1 7B and 13B, most layers). 13B holds up to 2,560 tokens. A random token sequence is only recoverable up to 128 tokens. A codebook of 256 input-output pairs is held reliably.
  setup: simplified input-independent LoReFT with a single scalar b, 4,097 parameters on 7B and 5,121 on 13B (about 17.5KB). 1000 epochs, learning rate 4e-3. Text is the start of Alice in Wonderland. Scrambled text recovers much worse.
  quote: "both models can successfully remember up to 2,048 tokens across most layers with a 100% recovery rate"
  where: App F.1-F.2, p.33-35. The authors note that pretraining memorisation of the book probably helps.

- Composition: different orthogonal subspaces of one LoReFT can be trained on different tasks, then used together.
  number: rank 8, split 4+4. Training took under 10 min on one A100 40G. 1K examples per task, 3 epochs.
  setup: LLaMA-7B. One half does German sentence completion (HellaSwag-DE variant), the other does instruction following (1K Ultrafeedback examples). Used together, the model answers in German. The evidence is qualitative only, with no metric and no tuning.
  where: App G.1, p.36-37

- Few-shot adaptation: LoReFT adapts a chat model to imitate GOODY-2 from 5 examples.
  number: 5 examples, rank-4 LoReFT at layer 15, 32,772 learned parameters, 100 epochs, under 30 seconds on an A100 40G
  setup: Llama-2-Chat. The result is qualitative only (a demo), and the paper includes a safety-use warning.
  where: App G.2, p.38

- Inference overhead exists and is small. Interventions are hooked into the forward pass and cannot be merged into the weights like LoRA's.
  number: about 0.05 second
  setup: LLaMA-1 7B, untrained LoReFT, 10 layers at rank 8 on the last prompt token, 256 generated tokens, greedy decoding.
  quote: "For intervening with 10 layers with a rank of 8 on the last prompt token, the overhead is about 0.05 second."
  where: App H, p.39

LIMITS
- Authors concede: mostly LLaMA-family models, with no other model families or vision-language models. The hyperparameter search space is large and not automated. Llama-3 8B was only run on commonsense. The authors do not know why ReFT works. The causal effect "may only emerge in the model's upstream computations".
- Arithmetic and chain-of-thought is the weak spot. Table 2 and App D.3 show losses to LoRA and adapters. The GSM8K gap is large.
- GLUE and instruction results are mixed. On GLUE, LoReFT does not beat LoRA on RoBERTa-base (84.2 vs 84.7). In Table 16, LoReFT's median is below VeRA and LoRA on RoBERTa-base (83.6 against 85.2 and 86.6), a comparison the authors put in the appendix because VeRA's protocol differs.
- Baseline numbers in the commonsense, arithmetic and instruction tables are taken from other papers (Liu 2024c, Hu 2023, Wu 2024a, Li 2023), not rerun under the same setup. The authors tuned on dev sets and say prior PEFT work tuned on test sets, so the comparisons are not exactly like for like.
- ReFT cannot be merged into the weights, unlike LoRA. Overhead is small but real (App H).
- The headline claim "more powerful ... than any existing PEFTs" (conclusion) is stronger than the tables support (see arithmetic).
- Dated: 2024 models only (LLaMA-1, Llama-2, Llama-3 8B). Nothing on RL or preference optimisation. Later PEFT work is not covered.

BUILDS ON
- Distributed interchange intervention and distributed alignment search: Geiger et al. 2023b; Wu et al. 2023. Causal abstraction and interchange interventions: Geiger et al. 2021, 2023a. Interchange intervention training (IIT): Geiger et al. 2022; Wu et al. 2022; Huang et al. 2023c.
- Representation editing and steering: RED (Wu et al. 2024a), activation addition (Turner et al. 2023), RepE (Zou et al. 2023), Li et al. 2024 (inference-time intervention). B.1-B.3 recast these as ReFT instances.
- Weight-based PEFT baselines: LoRA (Hu et al. 2022), DoRA (Liu et al. 2024c), adapters (Houlsby et al. 2019, Pfeiffer et al. 2020), prefix-tuning (Li and Liang 2021), BitFit (Ben Zaken et al. 2022), VeRA (Kopiczko et al. 2024).
- Experimental setups: Hu et al. 2023 (LLM-Adapters, commonsense and arithmetic), Wu et al. 2024a (RED, instruction tuning and GLUE). Library built on pyvene (Wu et al. 2024b).

CODE (App A, p.20; verbatim, but the extraction inserted spaces inside tokens)
reft_config = ReftConfig ( representations ={ "layer": 19, "component": "block_output", "intervention": LoreftIntervention ( embed_dim = model.config.hidden_size, low_rank_dimension =1) })
reft_model = get_reft_model ( model , reft_config )
Imports: from pyreft import get_reft_model, ReftConfig, LoreftIntervention, ReftTrainerForCausalLM. Repo: https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft

FIGURES (captions only, nothing rendered)
- Fig 1 (p.2): parameter count against performance for LoReFT and other PEFTs on four benchmarks (commonsense, arithmetic, instruction tuning, GLUE). Quickest view of the "far fewer parameters, similar or better score" claim.
- Fig 2 (p.4): ReFT intervention. Left panel shows an intervention at positions P in layer l. Right panel shows rank-2 LoReFT on 3-d states: project, replace the subspace component with Wh+b, add the edit back. Best picture of eq. 2.
- Figs 3-10 (p.34-35): memorisation heatmaps by layer and length, and the codebook test.
- Fig 11 (p.40): generation runtime against prompt length for varying rank, layers and positions.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF text. Extraction is clean apart from spacing artefacts in code and the equations (math symbols come out garbled), and a doubled "2" in the DiReFT row of Table 17 ("221.3", which should read 21.3). Table numbers come from the text extraction. I did not render any figures.
- Not read line by line: D.1 hyperparameter tables (p.23-28), B, C and I. Claims about them are not made here.
